text: Abstract:

Final Year Project (FYP) reports are frequently a very tedious and professional writing where students have to adhere to specific guidelines of the institutions. Formatting by hand takes up precious time, and distracts the actual research, and often the issue of inconsistencies ensues. The current project suggests creating an AI-driven Report Formatter that will automate the process of formatting the reports, making sure they are formatted in accordance with the institution-specific template and protecting the academic integrity. The system uses Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning to identify the elements of a document (headings, paragraphs, tables, figures and references) and uses these elements to apply formatting rules. An exclusive administration panel will enable the institutions to post and maintain their own templates to guarantee a high level of flexibility in the various universities. The innovations are AI-based with ethical vs. unethical image detection, which filters indecent or otherwise unacademic images, and a voice-activated formatting interface, which lets the user set formatting instructions by simply speaking to the computer and improving accessibility. Other functions provided are plagiarism and grammar check, absent section suggestions, and live preview. Word, PDF and LaTeX export options will be used to provide a high number of compatibility. The proposed solution alleviates the administrative workload of formatting, enhances academic integrity and increases accessibility in students by incorporating smart content classification and ethical protection as well as multi-modal interaction with users. In the end, the Report Formatter hopes to be a smart academic assistant that fills the gap between the creation of content and the presentation of the professional work, thus contributing to the high level of productivity and the quality of academic work in general.
Introduction

Report writing is part and parcel of academic and professional work. In tertiary education, learners have to deliver reports, theses, and project documentation which has to be in perfect format according to the requirements that are given by their institutions of higher learning. Such formatting guidelines usually include font types, font size, headings hierarchy, margin requirements, table format, reference format and other organizational aspects. Although these standards are required to ensure uniformity and readability, the manual formatting is normally time consuming, difficult and cannot be done without errors.

Students are often wasted in matching headings, numbering lists and the reference styles more than in the actual content of their work. The latter is even more difficult when the various institutions have varying formatting standards. As an example, one university might recommend using the APA style form of reference, and another one to use IEEE or Chicago style. Equally, the specifications on the appearance of the table, the position of the caption and the structure of the sections can be quite diverse. This is because the absence of a universal tool that can adapt to various formatting needs makes compliance quite challenging to the students, and in fact, unintentional non-compliance to institutional standards can be experienced. These difficulties are intensified in other group projects, where several contributors join their parts together in one document and in most instances the parts do not match.

Moreover, in the contemporary digital reports, figures and images may occasionally be included. Nevertheless, uncontrolled insertion of unethical or unacceptable images may affect academic integrity. In this way, not only do the quality of the content have to be properly formatted, but also the possibility to avoid the incorporation of unethical content into the academic records. As automation, artificial intelligence, and natural language processing become increasingly more dependable, there is a high demand on a smart solution that can automatize formatting, comply with ethical standards, and offer an opportunity to allow the user to define the formatting needs in flexible ways.
Problem Statement

Current report formatting processes are inefficient, error-prone, and time-consuming. Students often struggle with advanced formatting features in applications such as Microsoft Word and LaTeX. Additionally, institutions follow different formatting standards, making compliance difficult. Existing systems also lack mechanisms for ethical image detection, accessibility support through voice interaction, and intelligent automation. Therefore, there is a need for a smart system that automates formatting, classifies content intelligently, ensures ethical compliance, and supports multiple interaction methods.
Project Objectives
Application of Report Formatter system should bring about some gains:
Time Savings: The automation of the repetitive format process will save the students much time so that they can be able to spend the time on creating the content and conducting research.
Consistency and Accuracy: With automated formatting, the problem of human error will be removed, and the strict adherence to the requirements of the institution will be ensured.
Ethical Protections: The unethical image detection feature can be used to keep academic reports professional, ethical and devoid of unprofessional content.
Increased Accessibility - Speech-based input should allow users to create formatting rules via the voice, which will make the system more inclusive and easier to use.
Improved Quality: Grammar correction and plagiarism detector features will help in bettering the quality and originality of reports.
Collaboration Support: Teamwork in academic projects will be simplified with such features as version control and collaboration between people.
Flexibility and Adaptability: The system will support the different formatting rules and languages and therefore can be applicable across the various institutions and regions.
Flexibility: Compatibility with other academic submissions platforms, such as Word, PDF, and LaTeX document export capabilities will make it flexible.
Data Security: Vigorous privacy protocols will ensure that sensitive student reports are safe and they are not abused.

The purpose of this Report Formatter is, finally, to become a smart assistant to the students, researchers and institutions by creating a linkage between the content development, ethical adherence and professionalism. Using artificial intelligence, the system will not only enhance effectiveness of report writing, but also establish new levels of academic productivity, inclusiveness, and quality.
Proposed Methodology and Architecture
The system follows a modular AI-driven architecture consisting of:
Frontend Application (Flutter) for students and administrators.
Backend Services (Python/FastAPI or Django) for formatting and AI processing.
AI Modules for content classification, ethical image detection, grammar checking, and speech recognition.
PostgreSQL Database for storing templates, reports, and user data.
Document Processing Engine for generating formatted reports in Word, PDF, and LaTeX.
Methodology:
Users upload raw report files.
AI models classify document sections.
Formatting templates are applied automatically.
Additional services such as grammar checking, plagiarism checking, image ethics detection, and voice commands are processed.
A live preview is generated before exporting the final report.

Proposed Solution

The offered project, which will be called Report Formatter, presents an AI- and machine learning-based program that will be used to automate the process of report formatting based on the templates specified by the user or institutions. The system will include:
Admin Panel: It allows administrators to post and control format regulations like font styles, margins, table formats and heading structures. A custom template can be done by each university.
AI-Powered Content Classification: Detecting attributes (heading, subheading, tables, images, captions, references) and formats them accordingly
Ethical Image Detection: The system incorporates an AI model, which is capable of differentiating between ethical and unethical images.
Voice-Enabled Formatting Requirements: The users and administrators will be able to set formatting requirements by speech recognition using a microphone.
Student Application: This will enable students to post raw data (Word, PDF or plain text) and get a well formatted report according to the template of their campus.
Specialized: Grammar checking, plagiarism checking, table of contents auto-generated, audio and table numbering, section recognition, version control, collaboration, and multilingual.

Abstract

Academic documents such as reports, theses, and Final Year Project (FYP) documentation must follow strict institutional standards covering margins, fonts, heading hierarchy, captions, and frontmatter, and these standards differ from one institution to another. Beyond formatting, students must also ensure grammatical quality, structural consistency, appropriate images, and originality. However, general-purpose word processors leave template compliance to manual effort, causing inconsistent results, especially in group-written documents. Manual review by supervisors does not scale, and FYP supervision and shared version history are scattered across email, portals, and separate tools. This project presents FORMATIFY, a multi-tenant, AI-powered academic document quality and formatting platform built with a Flutter client, FastAPI backend, and SQLite, in which any institution can be onboarded as an independent organization and configure its own formatting templates, departments, deadlines, and modules. Documents uploaded as DOCX, PDF, text, Google Drive files, or through QR-based mobile upload are analyzed by specialized agents using Claude Haiku 4.5 or Gemini 2.5 Flash for text, local BLIP and CLIP models for images, and MinHash/LSH with MiniLM/FAISS for plagiarism detection. The AI only proposes issues; deterministic code applies approved fixes to the DOCX. Optional FYP management and collaboration modules are included. The implemented system delivers template-driven and freeform analysis, automated fixes, formatted DOCX export, isolated data per institution, supervisor review workflows, and section-based collaboration. FORMATIFY reduces formatting effort, improves consistency, and supports academic integrity across institutions.
Chapter 1 — Introduction
1.1 Overview

Academic documents such as reports, theses, dissertations, and Final Year Project (FYP) documents are required to follow specific institutional formatting standards. These standards may define document structure, margins, fonts, heading hierarchy, paragraph formatting, captions, tables, figures, frontmatter, and other presentation requirements. Although such standards provide consistency and professionalism, applying them manually can be time-consuming and may result in inconsistencies, particularly when documents are prepared collaboratively.

The problem becomes more complex when students are required to review not only the visual formatting of a document but also its grammatical quality, structural organization, image appropriateness, paragraph relevance, lists, and plagiarism. Supervisors may also need to review multiple student documents, monitor FYP submissions, provide feedback, and track project progress. Similarly, group projects require students to work on different sections while maintaining a consistent document structure and a reliable history of changes.

Existing general-purpose word processors provide extensive manual formatting functionality, but they do not automatically perform a complete academic document quality analysis according to institution-specific requirements. FORMATIFY addresses this gap by providing an AI-powered academic document quality and formatting platform that combines document analysis, institutional templates, automated fixes, image analysis, plagiarism detection, FYP management, and lightweight collaboration within a single system.

The implemented system follows a client-server architecture in which a Flutter desktop/mobile client communicates with a FastAPI backend. The backend manages document processing, AI analysis, authentication, organization-level access, document modification, FYP workflows, and collaboration services. SQLite is used for persistent storage, while organization-scoped records support the multi-tenant architecture.

FORMATIFY accepts DOCX, PDF, TXT, pasted text, Google Drive imports, and QR-based phone uploads. Depending on the selected institutional template, the system can perform template-driven or freeform analysis. The analysis covers grammar, formatting, heading structure, paragraph relevance, image ethics and relevance, tables, document lists such as TOC/LOT/LOF, and plagiarism. Identified issues can then be reviewed and appropriate fixes can be applied to a working DOCX document.

The platform also extends beyond document formatting through its optional FYP module. This module supports supervisor assignment, FYP groups, milestones, meeting notes, final submissions, plagiarism monitoring, and supervisor review. In addition, the collaboration module enables students to work on shared projects through section-based commits, merging, conflict resolution, and WebSocket-based presence.
1.2 Problem Statement

Academic document preparation requires students to satisfy multiple formatting and content-quality requirements simultaneously. Institutional templates may define margins, fonts, heading hierarchies, captions, frontmatter, tables, figures, and document lists, but these requirements are often applied manually and inconsistently. The problem becomes more significant when multiple students contribute different sections of the same academic document.

In addition to formatting, academic documents require review for grammar, structural consistency, paragraph relevance, image appropriateness, and plagiarism. Manual review of these aspects can require significant effort from both students and supervisors. The current FORMATIFY technical analysis identifies four major problems: inconsistent application of university templates, limited scalability of manual review, fragmented FYP management workflows, and the need for shared document history during group writing.

Another challenge is that general-purpose document editors do not provide institution-specific automated analysis. Students may know how to apply formatting manually but still overlook structural or consistency issues. Furthermore, FYP-related activities such as supervisor assignment, milestone tracking, submissions, meeting records, and review may be distributed across different communication channels and systems.

Group projects introduce an additional problem because different team members may independently modify different parts of a document. Without a lightweight mechanism for recording section changes and merging contributions, maintaining a consistent document and recovering previous versions can become difficult.

Therefore, there is a need for an integrated academic document platform that can analyze documents against institutional requirements, provide AI-assisted quality analysis, apply appropriate document fixes programmatically, support FYP management, and provide lightweight collaboration and version history.
1.3 Proposed Solution

FORMATIFY is proposed and implemented as a multi-tenant academic document quality and formatting platform that combines AI-assisted analysis with deterministic document processing. Students can upload a DOCX, PDF, TXT file, paste text, import a document from Google Drive, or upload a document through the QR-based mobile workflow. They can then select an institutional template or use the freeform analysis mode when a matching template is unavailable.

After document ingestion, FORMATIFY parses the document into an internal representation containing paragraphs, styles, tables, images, and related document structures. The content is divided into batches and analyzed through multiple specialized agents. These agents perform tasks such as grammar analysis, template formatting analysis, heading detection, paragraph relevance analysis, image ethics analysis, image relevance analysis, and plagiarism-related analysis.

The system uses Claude Haiku 4.5 as its primary language model, with Gemini 2.5 Flash available as an alternative configuration. For image understanding, FORMATIFY uses locally executed BLIP and CLIP models. Plagiarism detection combines MinHash/LSH for near-duplicate detection with MiniLM embeddings and FAISS for semantic similarity against an FYP corpus.

A key design decision is that the language model does not rewrite the complete academic document. Instead, the AI identifies and proposes issues, while deterministic backend components such as the reformatter and content fixer apply the actual changes to the working DOCX. This improves reproducibility and reduces the risk associated with allowing an LLM to regenerate an entire document.

The platform also provides institution-level administration through configurable templates and organization management. The FYP module provides supervisor assignment, milestones, meetings, submissions, plagiarism monitoring, and review workflows, while the collaboration module provides section commits, merging, conflict resolution, and real-time presence.
1.4 Main Objectives
Main Goal

To develop an AI-powered, multi-tenant academic document quality and formatting platform that assists students in analyzing and formatting academic documents according to institutional requirements while also supporting document quality assessment, FYP management, and collaborative academic work.
Specific Objectives
The specific objectives of FORMATIFY are:
To develop a template-driven academic document analysis system capable of evaluating documents against institution-specific formatting rules.
To implement freeform document analysis for users who do not have a suitable institutional template.
To develop AI-assisted analysis for grammar, formatting, heading structure, paragraph relevance, image ethics, image relevance, tables, lists, and document structure.
To implement local BLIP and CLIP-based image analysis for evaluating image ethics and relevance while avoiding dependence on cloud-based vision APIs.
To implement hybrid plagiarism detection using MinHash/LSH and MiniLM/FAISS-based semantic similarity against an academic/FYP corpus.
To develop deterministic document-processing mechanisms that can apply approved formatting and content fixes to a working DOCX document.
To develop a multi-tenant architecture that allows organizations to maintain separate users, templates, documents, and FYP-related data.
To implement role-based functionality for students, organization administrators, supervisors, and platform super administrators.
To develop an FYP management module supporting supervisor assignment, milestones, meeting notes, final submissions, plagiarism monitoring, and supervisor review.
To develop a collaboration and version-control-lite module that supports section-based commits, merging, conflict resolution, and project history.
To provide Google Drive integration and QR-based mobile document upload functionality for convenient document ingestion.
To provide a Flutter-based interface that supports both desktop and mobile workflows while keeping AI processing and document mutation on the backend.
1.5 Assumptions & Constraints
Assumptions
The organization administrator is assumed to configure the required institutional templates and formatting rules before students use template-driven analysis.
Users are assumed to provide accessible and valid document files for processing.
Users are assumed to have appropriate network connectivity when interacting with the FastAPI backend and cloud LLM services.
The configured AI services and required API credentials are available when cloud-based language analysis is performed.
Local BLIP and CLIP models are available to the backend and can be loaded during application startup.
Students using the FYP module are assumed to belong to an organization where the FYP module is enabled.
Users participating in collaboration projects are assumed to have the required accounts and project permissions.
Constraints
AI text analysis depends on the availability and configuration of the selected cloud LLM service.

Local vision models require sufficient computational resources and may increase application startup time; the technical documentation specifically notes that BLIP and CLIP are preloaded during backend startup.
Plagiarism detection primarily operates against the configured FYP corpus. Optional web verification exists but is disabled unless explicitly configured.
Direct integration with commercial plagiarism platforms such as Turnitin is not implemented.
LMS integrations such as Moodle or Blackboard are not implemented.
The system currently uses SQLite for persistence and is not documented as a cloud-deployed production service.
FYP-specific functionality is available only for organizations with the FYP module enabled.
Document analysis and formatting performance can vary according to document size, model availability, network conditions, and available computational resources.
1.6 Project Scope

The scope of FORMATIFY covers the development of a multi-tenant academic document quality and formatting platform consisting of a Flutter client and FastAPI backend. The system supports document ingestion through DOCX, PDF, TXT, pasted text, Google Drive, and QR-based phone upload mechanisms.

The core document-analysis scope includes template-driven and freeform analysis, grammar checking, formatting analysis, heading detection, paragraph relevance, image ethics, image relevance, table analysis, document lists, and plagiarism analysis. Users can review detected issues and apply supported fixes to a working DOCX document.

The project also covers institutional administration through configurable templates and organization-level management. Role-specific interfaces are provided for students, organization administrators, supervisors, and platform super administrators.

For FYP-enabled organizations, the scope includes supervisor assignment, group creation, milestones, deadlines, meeting notes, final submissions, plagiarism monitoring, notifications, and supervisor review/revision workflows.

The collaboration scope includes creation and joining of projects, section-based editing, commits, merging, conflict resolution, project member management, and WebSocket-based presence and section updates.

The project does not include direct Turnitin integration, LMS integration, or multilingual, fine-tuned document-classification, or LaTeX-export features unless these are separately verified as implemented.
1.7 Software Development Lifecycle Model

FORMATIFY follows an Agile Software Development Model. Agile is appropriate for the project because FORMATIFY consists of multiple interconnected components, including document processing, AI analysis, local computer vision, plagiarism detection, FYP management, collaboration, authentication, and institution-specific configuration. These components can be developed, tested, integrated, and refined incrementally.
The development process can be organized into iterative cycles involving requirements analysis, system design, implementation, testing, review, and refinement.
Development Phases
1) Requirements Gathering

The functional and non-functional requirements of students, administrators, supervisors, and other project stakeholders are identified and documented. Requirements include document analysis, template management, authentication, FYP workflows, plagiarism monitoring, and collaboration.
2) System Design

The system architecture, database structure, API design, document-processing pipeline, AI analysis architecture, role-based access control, and Flutter interfaces are designed. The implemented architecture uses Flutter on the client side, FastAPI on the backend, and SQLite for persistence.
3) Implementation

The system is implemented incrementally through its core components. These include document ingestion and parsing, AI analysis agents, deterministic document modification, image analysis, plagiarism detection, authentication, multi-tenancy, FYP management, collaboration, and external integrations.
4) Testing

Individual components and integrated workflows are tested to verify document analysis, authentication, organization isolation, FYP functionality, collaboration, and other system features. The repository contains unit-style tests and broader integration/functional tests covering areas such as multi-tenancy, authentication gates, FYP functionality, headings, lists, frontmatter, tables, and freeform analysis.
5) Deployment

The implemented system is configured as a Flutter client communicating with the FastAPI backend. The backend is run using Uvicorn, while the Flutter application's API configuration points to the backend host and port. Required environment configuration includes authentication, LLM, SMTP, and optional Google integration credentials.
6) Maintenance and Refinement

As an Agile project, identified defects, integration issues, performance concerns, and required refinements can be addressed iteratively. This allows the system to evolve as testing identifies issues in document processing, AI analysis, FYP workflows, or collaboration.
Chapter 2
Requirements Analysis
2.1 Literature Review

Academic report writing is an essential component of higher education. Students are required to produce structured, well-formatted documents that adhere strictly to the guidelines set by their respective institutions. These guidelines cover a wide range of formatting elements, including font styles and sizes, heading hierarchies, margin settings, table formats, caption placement, and reference styles. Despite the importance of consistent formatting, the process of manually applying these rules remains tedious, error-prone, and time-consuming for most students. As the demand for intelligent automation in educational tools grows, researchers and developers have increasingly explored how Natural Language Processing (NLP), document layout analysis, and computer vision can be combined to reduce this burden.
This section presents a review of existing tools, research studies, and technologies that are directly relevant to the development of FORMATIFY — an AI-based academic report formatting system.
Commercial Word Processors

Microsoft Word and Google Docs are the most widely used tools for academic writing. Both offer built-in styling features, template support, and basic formatting capabilities. However, as noted by Ahmad and Williams [12], these tools require users to apply formatting rules manually, which leads to inconsistency, especially in long, multi-authored documents. Neither system is capable of intelligently inferring the structural hierarchy of unformatted academic text or automatically adapting to institution-specific formatting requirements. The absence of any AI-driven formatting layer makes them insufficient as standalone solutions for the problem FORMATIFY aims to solve.
LaTeX and Overleaf

Overleaf, a cloud-based LaTeX editor, is widely adopted in academic and research communities for its ability to produce professionally typeset documents [15]. It supports real-time collaboration and enforces consistent document structure through its markup language. However, LaTeX requires users to learn a complex typesetting syntax, which presents a significant barrier for non-technical students. While it excels at structured document generation, it does not offer AI-powered flexibility — users must manually define all formatting rules and document elements. FORMATIFY draws inspiration from Overleaf's structured, rule-based approach to document generation but aims to eliminate the technical learning curve by automating the entire formatting pipeline.
AI-Based Language Models

Large language models such as GPT-based systems, including ChatGPT, have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generating and restructuring text. However, these models are not designed to enforce strict formatting conventions such as margin settings, page breaks, or caption positioning. They also lack a structured document layout analysis pipeline, which makes them unsuitable for template-driven, institution-specific report formatting. Rahman and Zhang [13] highlight that while such models can assist with content generation, they fall short when precise structural compliance is required.
Document Layout Analysis (DLA)

Document Layout Analysis is one of the most relevant research areas for FORMATIFY's content classification module. Xu et al. [16] introduced LayoutLM, a pre-trained model by Microsoft that combines textual and visual features to understand document structure, including titles, paragraphs, tables, and figures. Similarly, Li et al. [17] presented DocBank, a large-scale benchmark dataset designed for training document layout analysis models using weak supervision. Both of these works demonstrate that deep learning models can accurately identify structural elements within documents. FORMATIFY builds upon these foundations by applying similar classification techniques specifically in the context of academic report formatting, going further by integrating template compliance and multi-modal user interaction.
Grammar and Plagiarism Tools

Leemans et al. [18] evaluated the effectiveness of Grammarly as a writing assistance tool for students and found that it significantly improved grammatical accuracy and writing clarity. Similarly, Weber-Wulff [19] examined the strengths and limitations of plagiarism detection software, including Turnitin, which remains the industry standard for academic integrity checks. While both tools address content quality, neither offers any formatting automation or template compliance features. FORMATIFY plans to incorporate grammar and plagiarism checking capabilities as supplementary quality assurance features, complementing its core formatting engine.
Template Engines and Programmatic Document Generation

Programmatic document creation systems such as Jinja2, Apache POI, and python-docx enable developers to generate documents by filling predefined templates with structured data. These tools are effective for automation in controlled environments but are not adaptive — they cannot intelligently process unstructured academic text and map it to the appropriate template sections without explicitly defined rules. FORMATIFY goes beyond this by using NLP-based content classification to automatically identify and tag document elements before applying template rules.
Automated NLP-Based Formatting Systems

Islam and Rahman [20] proposed a prototype NLP-based formatting system that demonstrated the feasibility of using natural language processing to automatically parse and reformat academic documents. While this work confirmed that rule-driven NLP formatting is technically achievable, the system was limited in scope — it did not scale to handle diverse institutional templates and lacked support for ethical image detection. FORMATIFY directly addresses these limitations by building a more comprehensive, modular, and extensible system.
Ethical Image Detection

The inclusion of inappropriate or academically irrelevant images in student reports is a growing concern for academic integrity. Radford et al. [21] introduced CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pretraining), a multimodal model capable of classifying images based on natural language descriptions with high accuracy. Additionally, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) such as ResNet have been widely validated for image classification tasks, including content moderation. FORMATIFY incorporates an AI-powered ethical image detection module based on such models to automatically screen uploaded images and block any content that does not meet academic or professional standards — a feature entirely absent in all existing formatting tools.

Implementation Note: Of the directions surveyed above, the implemented FORMATIFY system confirms the Document Layout Analysis and ethical-image-detection directions in practice — structural classification is performed by a Claude-first heading-detection agent, and image screening runs locally using BLIP image captioning combined with CLIP (Radford et al. [21]) rather than a cloud vision API. Grammar and plagiarism checking (Leemans et al. [18]; Weber-Wulff [19]) is implemented as a hybrid pipeline: MinHash/LSH near-duplicate detection plus MiniLM/FAISS semantic matching against an FYP corpus, with an optional LLM pattern-hint stage. Text-reasoning tasks (grammar, formatting, headings, paragraph relevance) use Claude Haiku 4.5 or Gemini 2.5 Flash rather than a generic GPT-based assistant.
2.2 Stakeholders List

The project's stakeholders are both the direct and indirect users of the system who influenced the system design. The students and FYP Supervisors are the main users and interact with the system at every stage of the FYP process, ranging from being assigned a supervisor, submitting documents for review, receiving feedback and approval, to future students who will be using it in the next academic session. Configuration of the deadline management and supervision of the system are driven by Department Administrators, and are not predetermined based on assumptions. An external stakeholder, the University/FYP Committee, influenced key design decisions as their academic structure (the semester 6–7–8 FYP timeline) directly shaped the documentation tracking features of the system because there was no documentation artifact in semester 8, which is a committee defense. The development team is a stakeholder and the delivering party who is tasked to fulfil the needs of the end user and to fulfil the academic evaluation criteria of the FYP itself.
Students (FYP Group Members)

Primary User. Use the system to format reports, submit documentation (proposal, semester-7 documentation), track milestone/deadline status, communicate with supervisors, and manage FYP-related documents. Includes both current and future students who will use the system in subsequent academic sessions. Level of involvement: High — direct daily/weekly use throughout the FYP lifecycle.
FYP Supervisors

Primary User. Review and accept/reject supervision requests, review submitted documents, add paragraph-level comments, approve or request revisions on submissions, monitor plagiarism reports, and track assigned groups' progress. Includes both current and future supervisors. Level of involvement: High — core actor in the review and approval workflow.
Organization / Department Administrators

Administrative User. Manage organization-level configuration: create departments, add supervisor accounts (credentials emailed via SMTP), set department and semester 6/7 deadlines, create and edit institutional formatting templates (including extract-from-document), configure frontmatter branding assets, and view organization analytics/settings. Level of involvement: Medium-High — configures and governs workflow rules within their organization.
University / FYP Committee

External Stakeholder. Sets the broader academic structure the system must align with (6th-semester proposal, 7th-semester documentation, 8th-semester final defense); ultimately evaluates the FYP outside the system (particularly semester 8, which has no in-system documentation component). Level of involvement: Low-Medium — indirect influence via academic policy and calendar, not a direct system user.
Development Team (Project Authors)

Developer / Builder. Design, implement, test, and maintain the system (frontend, backend, AI-based formatting/plagiarism/grammar tools); responsible for meeting FYP evaluation criteria for this project itself. Level of involvement: High — full ownership of system design and delivery.
Platform Super Admin

Internal / Governing Stakeholder. Hidden platform-level role (accessed via a 5-tap gesture on the login screen, not an advertised link) that creates new organizations/tenants, seeds each organization's first admin account, sets organization plan and enabled modules (core/fyp), and views platform-wide statistics. Sits above individual organizations and is not exposed to students, supervisors, or organization admins. Level of involvement: High — controls onboarding and configuration of every tenant organization.
End-User Institutions (e.g., COMSATS)

Client / Adopting Organization. Adopting institution whose academic structure (departments, semester system, documentation requirements) the system is modeled around. Level of involvement: Medium — defines real-world requirements and constraints the system must satisfy.
Third-Party AI Service Providers

External/Technical Stakeholder. Provide underlying AI capabilities (e.g., heading detection, grammar checking, plagiarism analysis) that the system depends on via API integration. Level of involvement: Low — indirect, infrastructure-level dependency.
2.3 Requirements Elicitation

Requirements elicitation is the foundational step in the software development process through which the needs, expectations, and constraints of all stakeholders are identified and documented. For FORMATIFY, this process was carried out through a combination of document analysis, brainstorming sessions among team members, review of related literature, and observation of how students currently handle academic report formatting in their day-to-day university work.

Document Analysis was the primary elicitation technique used. The team carefully studied the official FYP report formatting guidelines provided by COMSATS University Islamabad, Lahore Campus, to understand exactly what formatting rules the system would need to enforce. This included analyzing heading structures, font requirements, margin specifications, table and figure caption placement, reference styles, and section organization standards.

Brainstorming Sessions were conducted among the three team members — Amna, Ayesha, and Eisha — along with feedback from their supervisor, Ms. Sana Rizwan. These sessions helped identify the core features the system must offer, optional advanced features such as ethical image detection, and the technical constraints the system would operate under.

Literature Review and Gap Analysis, as documented in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, also served as an important elicitation source. By studying what existing tools lacked, the team was able to define requirements that directly address those shortcomings — such as the need for institution-specific template adaptability and AI-powered content classification.

Observation of common student behavior during report writing revealed recurring pain points — such as time wasted on manual heading numbering, inconsistent font usage across group-contributed sections, and confusion around reference formatting — which directly informed several of the functional requirements listed below.

Through this combined elicitation process, the requirements were validated against the project's main goal: to build an AI-based academic report formatting system that is accurate, accessible, ethical, and institution-adaptive.

5.3 Tools and Technologies :

FORMATIFY is built as a multi-tenant, multi-layered stack consisting of a cross-platform Flutter client, an asynchronous FastAPI backend, a cloud LLM for text analysis, and locally-run AI models for image understanding and plagiarism detection. This section outlines the stack used in the final implementation.
Core Development Stack (Architecture)

Dart (Flutter 3.9+): Main framework for the cross-platform Desktop and Mobile client. The “one codebase, many platforms” approach ensures a consistent UI. The client does not embed any model weights; all AI processing and document modification run on the backend.
Provider, HTTP & app_links: Provider is used for state management, the HTTP package for communication with the backend REST APIs, and app_links for handling deep links such as formatify://qr-upload.
Python (3.11): Main language for backend development, AI model integration, and document processing.
FastAPI: Web framework used to build the “FORMATIFY API”. Its built-in support for asynchronous programming keeps the system responsive while heavy analysis tasks run.
Uvicorn: ASGI web server that serves the FastAPI backend.
SQLite: Relational database (formatify.db) that stores users, templates, documents, organizations, FYP records, and collaboration data. All tenant-specific data is scoped by org_id for multi-tenancy.
WebSockets: Used in the collaboration module for real-time member presence and section updates.
Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
Large Language Models (Text Analysis):

Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic): Default LLM for grammar checking, template-compliance checking, heading detection, paragraph relevance, and front-matter classification. It was chosen for its low latency, low cost for many batched calls, and strong adherence to structured JSON output.

Gemini 2.5 Flash (Google): Cost-effective alternative LLM, used when a Gemini API key is configured. A custom adapter keeps the Anthropic-style message format, so the same agents work with either model.
Computer Vision (Image Ethics & Relevance, run locally):
BLIP (Salesforce/blip-image-captioning-base): Generates captions for images, which are used for ethics checking and image–section relevance.
OpenAI CLIP (clip-vit-base-patch32): Performs zero-shot ethical-cue detection and measures image–text similarity for relevance checking.
Hugging Face Transformers: Library used to load and run the BLIP and CLIP models. Running them locally avoids per-image cloud vision costs and keeps students’ figures private.
Plagiarism Detection:
MinHash / LSH (datasketch): Detects near-duplicate (copy-paste) text through shingle matching.
Sentence-Transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2): Generates semantic embeddings of text.
FAISS: Performs fast similarity search of embeddings against the FYP corpus.
Google Custom Search (optional): Optional web verification stage, disabled by default.
Document Processing & Formatting Libraries
These libraries apply fixes and formatting programmatically. The LLM only identifies and labels issues, while the actual document changes are made by deterministic code.
python-docx: Reading, writing, and modifying Word (.docx) files according to template rules.
docxtpl: Template-based DOCX generation.
docxcompose: Merging DOCX documents (used for combining content such as front matter and merged collaboration documents).
PyMuPDF, pdfplumber & pypdf: PDF reading pipeline used to extract text in reading order, tables, and images from PDFs.
Authentication, Security & Integrations
Security:
JWT (PyJWT, HS256): Secure session management. The token carries user_id, org_id, role, email, and org_code, and is sent as a Bearer token.
Password hashing (SHA-256 with salt): Used for storing user passwords.
Role-based access control & Org Middleware: Resolves the tenant on each request (JWT, org code header, or API key) and restricts FYP-only routes to organizations that have the FYP module enabled.
Super Admin Key: Platform-level administration is protected by a secret key (X-Super-Admin-Key) kept in the environment configuration.
Integrations:
Google Drive (google-api-python-client + OAuth 2.0): Import of files from Google Drive; Google Docs are exported to DOCX.
SMTP (smtplib / EmailMessage): Sends emails for supervisor credentials, organization admin credentials, and collaboration invite codes.
QR-based phone upload: A deep-link and session-based mechanism that allows documents to be uploaded from a phone to the desktop app.
Hardware Requirements (Development & Inference Environment)
Processor: At least an Intel Core i5 (10th Gen) or AMD Ryzen 5.
RAM: 16 GB recommended, to run the Flutter development environment together with the backend and the local BLIP/CLIP/MiniLM models.
Graphics: An NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support is optional and speeds up local vision inference (BLIP/CLIP).
Internet: Required for the cloud LLM (Claude / Gemini) and for Google Drive integration.
5.4 Implementation Details

FORMATIFY was developed in a systematic, sprint-based approach following the Agile methodology, where each module was developed, tested, and refined in subsequent sprints. The final implementation is a multi-tenant academic document quality and formatting platform with role-specific interfaces for students, organization admins, supervisors, and a platform super admin.
System Architecture
FORMATIFY follows a client–server architecture, organized into the following layers:
Presentation Layer: A Flutter (Dart) application for desktop and mobile, with separate role-based dashboards for students, organization admins, supervisors, and the super admin.

Application Layer: A FastAPI server (served by Uvicorn) that exposes the REST APIs. An organization middleware resolves the active tenant on every request and restricts FYP-only routes to organizations that have the FYP module enabled.

AI & Analysis Layer: Analysis agents that run in parallel, including grammar, formatting, heading detection, paragraph relevance, image ethics, and image relevance. They use a cloud LLM (Claude Haiku 4.5 or Gemini 2.5 Flash) for text analysis and local models (BLIP, CLIP) for image analysis. A separate plagiarism package handles plagiarism detection.
Document Processing Layer: Deterministic services (reformatter, content_fixer, heading_analysis, and image and table services) that apply fixes to a working DOCX copy.
Data Layer: A SQLite database (formatify.db) in which all organization-specific tables carry an org_id. Uploaded and working files are stored in the server’s uploads directory.
The Flutter app does not contain any model weights. All AI processing and document modification run on the backend.
Multi-Tenancy and Module Gating

FORMATIFY supports multiple organizations (universities or companies) on a single platform. Each organization has its own plan, enabled modules, document quota, and branding. The organization middleware identifies the tenant from the JWT claims, an organization-code header, or an API key. Two modules are defined: core (document analysis and formatting) and fyp (Final Year Project management). Organizations without the FYP module cannot access the supervisor, student FYP, and deadline routes. Email and username uniqueness are scoped per organization.
Authentication and Access Control

Users sign up or log in by entering their organization code, which is resolved through the backend. On login, the server verifies the password (hashed with SHA-256 and a salt) and issues a JWT (HS256) that contains the user ID, organization ID, role, email, and organization code. This token is sent as a Bearer token with every request. Access is role-based: students use the formatting and FYP tools, admins manage templates, users, and settings, and supervisors manage their groups and submissions. The platform super admin interface is protected by a secret key (X-Super-Admin-Key) and is opened through a hidden gesture on the login screen (five taps on the Formatify logo).
Document Upload and Processing

Students can add documents in several ways: uploading a DOCX or PDF file, pasting text or uploading a TXT file, importing from Google Drive (OAuth), or uploading from a phone through the QR-based mobile flow. A freeform mode is also available for documents that do not follow any institutional template, where template section-order checks are skipped.

A parser converts every input into an internal document model containing paragraphs (with styles and IDs), tables, and images. PDFs are read using PyMuPDF, with pdfplumber and pypdf as fallbacks, and text lines are merged into proper paragraphs while tables and images are kept in reading order.
Analysis Pipeline
Each analysis job passes through the following stages:
The document is parsed.
Front matter (cover page, certificates, etc.) is excluded from scoring.
The content is split into batches by page and text density, with overlap to preserve context.
The analysis agents and the plagiarism pipeline run in parallel on the batches.
An aggregator merges all findings into a single analysis report.
A formatted DOCX is generated for download.
The document analysis screen also runs heading detection and prepares a DOCX working copy, so that fixes always refer to stable paragraph IDs.
AI Analysis Modules

Grammar and Formatting Analysis: The LLM checks grammar, spelling, and punctuation, and checks template compliance based on each template’s required sections and formatting rules. In freeform mode, general academic formatting rules are used instead.
Heading Detection: Heading candidates are first detected by the LLM. Uncertain candidates are shown to the student, who can Keep or Discard them.
Paragraph Relevance: Checks whether a paragraph belongs under its heading.

Image Ethics Detection: Images are captioned locally with BLIP, and ethical and academic appropriateness is assessed using a taxonomy and CLIP zero-shot cues. No cloud vision API is used, which keeps students’ figures private.
Image Relevance Detection: CLIP measures the semantic similarity between an image and the section it appears in (with BLIP captions), so irrelevant images can be flagged.

Plagiarism Detection: A hybrid approach is used. MinHash/LSH catches near-duplicate text first, then MiniLM sentence embeddings with FAISS find semantic matches against the FYP corpus. Optional LLM-based AI-writing pattern hints and optional web verification are available, both disabled by default.
Document Formatting and Fixes

The LLM only identifies and labels issues. The actual changes are applied by deterministic code, which makes formatting reproducible and avoids the risk of the LLM rewriting the whole document. Students can apply a single fix, apply all fixes, or apply style fixes, and then download the formatted DOCX. The system also handles image formatting, table formatting, and the generation of the Table of Contents, List of Tables, and List of Figures. Front-matter pages (cover page, etc.) can be analyzed and generated using the institution’s branding.
Student Application

The student dashboard contains Home, New Report, My Reports, Collaboration, Templates, Settings, and Notifications, plus FYP tabs when the module is enabled. In New Report, the student selects a template (or skips it), chooses the upload source, and proceeds to the analysis screen. The analysis screen shows staged progress and organizes results into tabs: Review, Grammar, Formatting, Image Ethics, Image Relevance, Tables, Paragraph Relevance, Plagiarism, and Document Lists (TOC/LOT/LOF).
FYP Module

When the FYP module is enabled, the following lifecycle is supported: the admin creates departments, supervisors, and deadlines; the student sends a supervisor request; the supervisor accepts it and a group is created; the student views milestones, meeting notes, plagiarism reports, and a status tracker; and the student submits the final document. The supervisor reviews each submission (approve, request revision, or reject), monitors plagiarism, writes meeting notes, and comments on paragraphs. In-app notifications keep both sides updated.
Version Control and Collaboration Module

Students can create or join a project and invite members through an emailed invite code. A base document is split into sections, and members commit edits to sections. The module supports commit history, rollback to a previous version, merging, and conflict resolution on a dedicated merge screen, after which the merged DOCX can be downloaded. A WebSocket connection provides real-time presence and section updates.
Mobile Companion and QR Upload

A QR-based session allows a student to upload a document from a phone to the desktop workflow, using deep links (formatify://qr-upload and formatify://qr-download). The mobile screens also support downloading the formatted document to the phone.
Admin Dashboard Implementation

Dashboard Architecture and UI: The admin dashboard is part of the Flutter app, with a separate page for each feature: Overview, Departments, Users, Template Manager, Analytics, Verify Files, and Settings. FYP-specific pages (Supervisor Management, Deadlines, Semester Deadlines, Universities) are shown only when the FYP module is enabled. The backend is configured through environment variables (API keys, JWT secret, SMTP, Google OAuth).

Template Management: Admins create and manage institutional templates through the Template Manager and its configuration screen, defining required sections, formatting rules, and image, table, and list rules. Templates can also be created, updated, and deleted through the admin APIs. A template can be extracted automatically from an institution’s guideline DOCX, which pre-fills the rules. Front-matter branding and assets are also configured here.
User and Supervisor Management: Admins manage users and departments and add supervisors, whose temporary credentials are sent by email through SMTP.

Super Admin: The platform super admin creates and manages organizations (plan, modules, active status) and views platform statistics. When an organization is created together with an admin, the organization code and login credentials are emailed to that admin.

Abstract

GoMate serves users with an efficient application that delivers cost-efficient and environmentally friendly transportation solutions. Members can choose between individual rides or ride-sharing, where multiple users can join a single ride when their drop-off and pick-up destinations match. GoMate promotes shared rides as its primary goal to reduce road traffic by minimizing fuel usage and cutting down emissions which enables better environmental sustainability in urban settings. GoMate focuses first on smart ride matching and route optimization to minimize driver off-route trips together with improved trip effectiveness. The platform combines Google Maps for current geo-location features with Google OR-Tools to determine the most efficient and economical routing paths. The system applies a programmed workflow design to deliver effective ride management functions. Users submit ride requests through the platform which records their necessary trip information such as their starting and ending locations. The system possesses an intelligent and efficient algorithm using which it matches the riders with similar route and then optimizes the routes for efficient ride-hailing service. The fare system of GoMate includes dynamic calculations that combine route lengths with participation rates to offer reasonable prices for city travelers. Environmental sustainability acts as the fundamental driving force for the development of GoMate. The growing awareness about climate change together with urban air pollution problems makes excessive solo rides responsible for a substantial increase in greenhouse gas outputs. GoMate promotes shared rides between users as it reduces emissions footprints and assists municipalities in adopting environment-friendly transportation systems. Moreover, lessened number of vehicles leads to reduced traffic congestion which results into shorter travel times and better fuel efficiency. Development of GoMate integrates usability with security as fundamental priorities. Seamless user authentication through the platform enables convenient boarding for all users. Through real-time monitoring features GoMate delivers more transparent tracking of both trips and arrival predictions to its users. The success of GoMate include precise ride matching, efficient real-time tracking and user contentment. The integration of technology with sustainability allows GoMate to reform urban commuting with its smart and cost-effective and environmentally friendly transportation system.

Chapter 1: Introduction
Introduction

Digital technologies have significantly improved transportation systems in past decades. Existing ride-booking platforms like Uber and Careem have made travelling convenient by providing quick access to transportation services. However, several challenges like high fares, traffic congestion, low vehicle utilization and long waiting times remain unsolved. In addition, many individuals and businesses struggle to find affordable and reliable delivery services for packages across the city.

Traditional ride-hailing platforms have largely improved the travel experience, but their primary focus is on individual rides. This arises a gap in market for shared commuting. Shared commuting is not only environmentally friendly but also fuel-efficient and cost-effective. Unfortunately, majority of existing services do not prioritize route optimization and ways to minimize fuel consumption by reducing driver detours. Furthermore, delivery services are typically managed by separate platforms. This makes users rely on multiple applications for different needs. These gaps highlight the need for a more integrated and intelligent transportation solution that saves time, reduces costs, and enhances the overall user experience.

We introduce GoMate, a smart and user-friendly mobile application to address these challenges. GoMate includes ridesharing services, reducing travel costs, saving fuel, and improving ride availability. GoMate offers users two ride options: a solo ride, where a user can book a private ride, and a ride-sharing option, which matches users traveling in similar directions.The ride-sharing feature is powered by a proximity-based matching algorithm, which pairs users based on their pickup location and the driver’s route. This ensures minimal detours for drivers, allowing both passengers to reach their destinations comfortably and on time.

To sustain a manageable scope of development, the GoMate project lacks some advanced and large-scale features. This version does not include AI-based functions like predicting demand or intelligent ride assignment, etc. Also there is no additional safety features such as emergency SOS, live-ride sharing with friends and contacts, and automatic background checks of drivers. Secondly, GoMate lacks loyalty or reward programs, multi-city support, corporate/fleet booking, and audio/video recordings during rides. These parts are out of the intended scope of this project and can be regarded in the future improvements.

GoMate offers numerous benefits for its users. It provides a cost-effective and flexible commuting solution for passengers. It increases earning opportunities by reducing idle time and enabling more rides or deliveries per trip for drivers. Moreover, our goal is to reduce traffic congestion, fuel consumption, and harmful emissions by promoting ridesharing and route optimization. The application contributes to sustainable urban mobility.

Overall, GoMate is not merely a ride-booking app; it is an all-purpose solution of urban mobility that provides all the features of both ridesharing and personal rides to a one-stop and user-friendly application. GoMate will make everyday travel enjoyable by embedding convenience, effectiveness, and flexibility in an effort to revolutionize the manner in which commuters, students, and professionals environmentally use their travels. The clean design, smart functionality, real-time location tracking, smart route optimization and user-friendly interface make the platform more accessible and reduces the time and cost of traveling. Besides, GoMate promotes ecology through commuting by sharing rides, minimizing vehicle traffic, and consequently leading to decrease in carbon emission. Its emphasis on low cost, sustainability, and safety of users makes GoMate a progressive solution to the contemporary urban transport issues.
Problem Statement

Metropolitan transportation systems within cities struggle because of the population increase while fuel usage elevates, and road congestion deteriorates. Traditional ride-hailing operations generate excessive road traffic by serving mostly individual passengers thus causing major air pollution and fuel waste. The pattern results in increased transportation expenses for people commuting while also creating more environmental stress because of boosted carbon dioxide releases. This issue becomes a reality because existing transportation networks lack adequate ride-sharing systems. The majority of ride-hailing platforms provide private ride services but do not prioritize shared ride options as their standard offering. Sub-optimal ride-matching abilities and routing systems cause vehicles to travel with empty seats thus wasting fuel and creating longer trips.
Proposed Solution

GoMate establishes an optimized ride-sharing system which promotes users to join shared travel when routes coincide between each other. GoMate analyses the real time data, perform the ride matching for the riders and utilizes the intelligent optimization algorithms to choose the optimized route for their travel and reduce the travel detours to provide fuel-efficient, cost-effective and eco-friendly transportation mode for the people.

GoMate uses modern technologies to make the system effective and reliable. The application utilizes the Google Maps API for real-time location tracking and route visualization while optimizeing routes to ensure drivers take the shortest and most efficient paths. The backend is developed using NestJS, which handle business logic, user data, and ride management. The mobile app front end for drivers and riders is built using React Native while the front end for admin is built using Next.js. All data, including user profiles and ride history, is securely stored in a MongoDB database, which also supports location-based data processing.
Main Objectives
The GoMate platform focuses on delivering sustainable and inexpensive ridesharing services to users. Its main objectives include:
Providing Multi-Modal Services: A system that offers the choice of personal one-on-one driving service and car sharing service.

Implementing an Intelligent Matching System: Development of a system that associates the users within the shortest distance and their direction of travel, to further reduce distance covered and improve on the convenience of consumers of ride sharing services.

Integrating Advanced Route Optimization: Integration of geolocation service and the best route planning algorithm to determine the shortest, most cost-effective route that shall in turn benefit both drivers and users through shorter time and fuel consumption.
Ensuring Real-Time Updates: Display of real time GPS tracking, distance-based fare structure and live status updates to keep users informed at all times in a journey.

Enhancing Urban Mobility and Sustainability: Building sustainable networks for greener cities by endorsing the sharing of the means of transportation to help decrease the traffic jam and pollutant emissions in cities.

2.1.3 Sustainability-oriented route generation for ridesharing services

The research develops efficient ridesharing routes through multi-objective optimization which uses Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA3) from Genetic Algorithms (GA). The new approach reduces passenger travel duration along with waiting delays and unnecessary distance travel and environmental footprint without compromising driver activity equality. This approach differs from standard greedy routing since it creates multiple feasible solutions so customers may choose according to their preferences. Performance assessment of the system occurs with genuine data from Didi which shows improvements across ride-sharing rates and operational efficiency metrics alongside environmental emissions reductions. The research shows that larger vehicle capacity creates more opportunities for ride sharing which produces decreased pollution levels and minimalizes expenses for passengers. This research demonstrates how AI optimization helps sustainable transportation management while showing different elements which impact ridesharing efficiency. 2.1.8 Pricing in Ride-Share Platforms: A Queueing-Theoretic Approach

The research evaluates the cost-benefit analysis of price adjustments which depend on current supply and demand conditions versus fixed fares persisting over time. The authors incorporate stochastic models that take into account driver and passenger behaviour patterns for analysing how both pricing strategies deal with system fluctuations. According to the research results static pricing which reaches optimal levels proves superior to dynamic pricing strategies because it delivers higher throughput and revenue. Dynamic pricing continues to be commonly utilized in the market because of its ability to adapt to market uncertainties together with its capability to maintain equilibrium despite demand uncertainties. The research applies its mathematical model across multi-region networks to study the diverse demands for rides between regions. Research investigates driver-passenger interactions to better understand how these relationships affect the development of optimal pricing strategies while uniting with other matching market and revenue management studies. The paper creates essential understanding of pricing models that impact operational effectiveness in ride-sharing platforms to provide foundation knowledge for platform development in the future.

2.1.11 Hybrid ridesharing algorithm based on GIS and ant colony optimization

This study investigates Tehran while it uses the geosocial network platform Telegram for user engagement. The system architecture implements three sequential operational procedures starting with K-means algorithm-based passenger spatio-temporal clustering followed by Voronoi Continuous Range Query (VCRQ) and Region Connected Calculus (RCC5) together with Allen’s Temporal Interval Algebra for passenger-driver matching then applying Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) to optimize shared routes. Real-time data about traffic and speed information from vehicles enhances the operational efficiency of the model alongside user satisfaction. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that shared transportation grows longer and takes less time and involves more passengers collaborating with existing systems. The study identifies constraints in its ability to lower the expenses of taxi services and ridesharing. The study suggests future development elements should include flexible wait times with demographics-based individual matching. Smart urban mobility gets enhanced through GIS application with metaheuristic optimization which outcomes in decreased traffic congestion and fuel usage and environmental protection.

Implementation Details

Once the tools, technologies, and frameworks were selected, the GoMate application was built in a structured, systematic manner by implementing the proposed system into a real-world functional application.
5.4.1 System Architecture
The architecture of the system was modularized, and the separation of concerns was applied to the rider app, driver app, admin panel, backend services, and database.
Rider App: Utilized React Native for Presentation Layer.
Driver App: Utilized React Native for Presentation Layer.
Admin Panel: Utilized Next.js for Presentation Layer.
Backend APIs: Utilized NestJS for Application Layer.
Database: Utilized MongoDB for the Data Layer
5.4.2 Rider App Implementation
Reusable UI:

React Native/Expo follows a component-based and modular design. Layouts and functionality (like Parity input fields and buttons, modals, themed text and views) are implemented as reusable UI components, and are used on multiple screens. Screens are responsible for processing the data and displaying it in UI components. The presentation is styled with Tailwind CSS and a global stylesheet to give designers and developers a common design system to easily maintain the UI.
User Authentication:

NestJS and JWT are used to securely log in their users by using tokens. The back end provides end points to handle login and registration, verify credentials using bcrypt as well as issue JWT tokens to users with authentication. NestJS AuthGuard and role-based access controls are used to provide security to protected routes to ensure that users can access the specific resource only when they have access rights. Secrets are environment based and offer a secure token signature.
Location and Map Handling:

Pickup and drop-off points are handled based on GeoJSON coordinate constructs that are stored on MongoDB. The geospatial queries are carried out to find out nearby drivers in an efficient way and the map interactions like geocoding are managed on the client-side with the help of helper functions. This enables the application to offer precise location applications and live driver matching.
Solo Ride:

In solo rides, the passengers place ride requests using specific screens. The backend stores a new ride request, performs geospatial queries to identify nearby drivers and informs them in real time with the help of WebSockets. Offers and rides can be sent or accepted by drivers and the status is updated once a ride is accepted and this notifies both the driver and the passenger.
Shared Ride:

For shared rides, the solo case is extended with additional matching logic. This includes finding compatible riders, bundling shared trips, and generating dual-rider offers and notifications. This allows for efficient ride-sharing, with real-time updates to all parties involved.
Real-Time Communication:

For real-time communication, ride offers, status changes and notifications are delivered to clients using Socket. IO and the NestJS WebSocket gateways. The backend handles the passenger and the driver connecting, processing incoming ride requests, counter-offers and ride progress through a socket connection while emitting specific outputs, the frontend establishes a socket connection and updates the UI of the application accordingly
5.4.3 Driver App Implementation
Driver Verification Functionality:

The driver verification frontend is built with Expo and React Native (TypeScript). It used modular screens and form components. Image capture and selection is done with Expo ImagePicker/Camera, with all previews being custom UI components. Form data is sent as multipart/form-data to the back end with fetch or axios, and state management and validation are implemented with React hooks.
Route Optimization:

Route and map displays are built using React Native MapView and directions are retrieved from external Directions APIs (e.g. Google Maps) via an HTTP request. Polylines, routes, ETAs and distances are calculated on the client and passed to map and UI components which update the driver interface accordingly.
Solo Ride:

The driver app solo ride front end is also powered by Socket.IO client to proximate to the server-side NestJS WebSocket gateway. Local React state and hooks provide real-time changes to the UI of ride requests, offer submissions and ride status changes. Components like bottom cards, ride list, ride detail modal, etc are built in a modular fashion to render real time incoming rides and interactions between the driver and the ride.
Shared Ride:

Shared ride frontend is based on the same Socket.IO infrastructure used, and some other modular components manage multi-passenger rides. The state management provides coordination of offers and updates of group rides across the UI based on the use of the same bottom cards, ride lists and modals.
5.4.4 Admin Dashboard Implementation
Dashboard Architecture & UI:

The admin dashboard is built as a standalone web application using Next.js (App Router) and TypeScript). It follows a modular, page-based structure where each feature (dashboard overview, drivers management, analytics) is implemented as a separate route under /dashboard. Client-side rendering is used for quick UI updates, and reusable components such as cards, tables, charts, and search bars form the main layout. Environment variables configure backend communication, allowing the admin panel and NestJS server to run independently.
Data Fetching & API Communication:

All dashboard data—such as stats, driver lists, ride counts, or analytics—is fetched from the NestJS backend using REST APIs. Pages use useEffect and React hooks for data loading, error handling, and local UI state updates. When admins perform actions (e.g., toggle driver status), the dashboard sends PATCH or DELETE requests to the backend. Successful responses update the UI instantly, while errors (like “Unauthorized” or validation failures) are clearly shown using inline messages or logs.
Analytics, Charts & Reporting:

The dashboard includes charts for trends such as monthly rides vs. revenue, built with dual-axis visualizations so both small and large values remain visible. Status-based charts (e.g., active vs. inactive drivers) display system distribution using a consistent color palette. Summary cards show real-time counts of users, drivers, rides, and total revenue. All analytics are fetched from /admin/dashboard/ endpoints and rendered dynamically.
Driver Management & CRUD Operations:

The /dashboard/drivers page provides complete driver management functionality. A searchable table lists driver details including name, phone, vehicle, status, and ride count. Admins can activate/deactivate drivers with a single toggle, which sends a status update to the backend and refreshes the row state. The page supports client-side filtering, real-time updates after actions, and clean error handling. The design is fully extensible for future CRUD operations like editing or removing drivers.
5.4.5 Backend Implementation
API Structure:

Backend is developed with NestJS and TypeScript and the code is structured as controllers used to define REST endpoints, services to house business logic, and Mongoose for MongoDB persistence. DTOs and class-validator are used to authenticate inputs and JWT and role based guards are used for authentication/authorization. Environment variables are used for configuration/secrets.
Ride Matching Algorithm:

Ride matching algorithm leverages Mongoose queries and MongoDB geospatial features (2dsphere). By using GeoJSON indexing for driver locations and geospatial querying to identify nearby drivers, algorithm finds surrounding drivers with geospatial queries filtered by ride type and availability. Solo rides are grouped by proximity first, while combined rides attempt to combine multiple requests in groups based on overlapping routes and compatibility with each other to form multi-passenger trips.
Fare Calculation Algorithm:

Computation of fares is done on the server written in TypeScript. Distances and time are used to calculate fares with configurable parameters, which include base fare, amount per distance, amount per time, and multiplier by type of ride. Estimates of calculated fares are forwarded back to the client as round numbers.
Real-Time WebSocket Server:

The use of a NestJS Socket.IO gateway to communicate in real-time is used with the connection to the clients through socket.io-client. The gateway handles drivers and passengers connected to it, processes ride events, and broadcasts desired updates. State of the temporary ride can be stored in memory until persisted and the authentication is provided by using token-based handshakes.

5.6 Challenges During Implementation
In the process of developing GoMate some technical issues arose especially because of the complexity of dealing with real time ride-sharing, cross platform integration and dependencies of the system.
SDK Version Compatibility:

The other teammates were using SDK 53 and another one had updated to SDK 54 that resulted in compatibility problems. The dependencies varied, the methods were outdated and new libraries failed to build and resulted in errors at runtime. These problems had to be resolved by carefully synchronizing SDK versions, dependency management and code modifications to ensure both development environments would behave consistently.
Shared Ride Implementation:

The application of the shared ride feature was to be simulated with multiple riders on different devices. Linking two rider phones to the development system to test shared ride requests brought difficulties in balancing real-time information, processing of seat reservations, and consistent ride information that both riders would see. The multi-user requests and the correct updating of the ride status needed a thorough testing and debugging to prevent conflicts and mismatch in the shared ride workflow.
WebSocket Issues of real-time updates:

WebSockets were used in GoMate to allow real-time interaction between the riders and drivers, such as ride requests, real-time location tracking, and negotiating the prices. As part of the development, a number of problems were experienced, including delayed delivery of messages, loss of connection, and delayed state updates especially when there were a lot of users connected at the same time. The problems that were to be debugged included optimizing the backend event handling, proper reconnection strategy and testing in various network conditions to ensure real time communication remains stable.
Code Reusability and Modularity:

The other important issue in GoMate implementation process was the reusable code that was to be modular. It was important to make elements in a manner that reduced redundancy since through various features such as solo rides, shared rides, negotiating fares, ride tracking, and authentication had to be done in both rider and driver applications. Firstly, certain capabilities were being duplicated in various modules, thereby making them harder to maintain and prone to inconsistency. It took time and testing to refactor the code in order to make it reusable and shared services and modular components.

Nevertheless, these technical issues notwithstanding, these incompatibilities related to SDKs, reliable WebSocket communication, and extensive testing of shared ride situations allowed the core functionality of GoMate to be implemented effectively and made the process of working with it efficient and smooth for both the rider and the driver.
Chapter 6: Conclusions
6.1 Summary

GoMate is a two-app ride-hailing product that offers riders and drivers solo ride and ride-sharing services via two distinct apps. The rider app has the ability to book rides, input the pickup and destination addresses, propose prices, track drivers in real time and view ride history, whereas the driver app has the ability to create an account with documents verified, accept and send ride requests, view fares and manage rides in progress and completed rides. The system has the ability to intelligently match the riders and the drivers according to their proximity, availability, and the fare preferences so that the booking is not complicated. GoMate provides a variety of advantages such as the ability to reduce the travel expenses by taking a ride together, as well as increase the efficiency of the route by tracking and optimization with real-time data, more flexibility to the drivers with the ability to negotiate fares, and convenience in general to the users. Besides, the platform contributes to the reduction of traffic congestion and sustainable urban transportation, which provides an effective, flexible, and user-friendly mobility solution.
